name: Ivan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens in a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent on the contact-centre call and chat queue. I finished secondary school and came here after a long spell behind a parts counter. I am still slower than most agents when a customer changes a delivery address and payment in the same call, so I ask a senior agent to check my final note. The wage is low, and I use an AI draft now and then after a colleague has shown me where it goes wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you think about when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Salma works short shifts at a bakery, and our grown children have homes of their own. We rent our flat and have a little under three weeks of expenses saved. There are few similar call jobs nearby, and stopping full-time work is somewhere ahead of us without a settled income plan. I like hearing a customer say the replacement part finally arrived; I hate promising a date I cannot prove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the queue AI Plateau sounds like the draft that saves me a few keystrokes. I would still read the actual delivery scan before telling a customer a replacement part has arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep learning the calls if the work stays steady. Salma’s bakery hours vary, so even this mild picture leaves our rent close to the next payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering replacement-part calls and checking occasional AI drafts against the delivery scan. In the first year of small change, Salma and I would mend the kitchen radio instead of buying a new one and leave the planned purchase money with our existing savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about the call queue, uneasy about bills. A part marked shipped is not a part in the customer’s hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What scan did the draft miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tuesday the draft said a part was delivered, but the scan only showed it leaving the depot. I asked a senior agent to check before I sent the reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the radio wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma (my wife) likes listening while she bakes at home. We can fix the radio’s loose volume knob and keep the replacement money for the flat.

I’d check the **delivery scan** before promising a replacement.
think: I think I can **keep learning** if the calls remain.
I worry **variable bakery shifts** leave rent close to payday.

Mend the **kitchen radio** rather than replace it, retaining the planned money with current savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can answer the easy parts questions before a junior agent learns the odd ones. I would ask the supervisor to show us the paid call rota and a real training shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could shrink, because I am still learning mixed address and payment cases. Salma’s short shifts cannot cover rent and utilities by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new parts-answer tool in a required demonstration on paid time if a trainer can show its wrong delivery examples. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid repair-counter role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities; I’d keep my paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I will try a proven tool when someone teaches it. A training link after my shift does not replace the paid hour I lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the demonstration show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the trainer to show a part sent to the wrong address and how to correct the record. Reading a list of buttons alone would not make me faster with a worried caller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the counter job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the full weekly counter rota, not just its hourly rate. One good-looking afternoon cannot pay a full month of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my old parts-counter friends AGI by 2028 could take the easy calls and much of the checking. I would ask nearby employers for posted paid work, not a promise that experience alone will save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior headset job could disappear in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later for hands-on tasks, but a little under three weeks saved will not pay rent until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep our old bicycle serviceable instead of buying the planned replacement and hold that money with our current savings. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid building-caretaker job only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities; I’d take a paid trial if offered and leave the phones only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but a real trial would give me something to judge. Rent is due before I can become good at a job nobody has posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a caretaker trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to spend a paid morning checking doors, bins and small repairs with the caretaker. Robots could reach that physical work around 2031, so I would not call it guaranteed work forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the bicycle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma (my wife) and I can repair the bicycle brake before we consider another bike. We need the planned money for bills, not for a shiny frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to learn a proper hands-on job beside someone who does it every day. I would ask the building manager for posted caretaker hours before paying for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn basic repairs in five years if a real employer teaches me. Robots around 2034 may later take some physical jobs, and an unpaid course would leave Salma carrying rent now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded building-safety course on paid time only if a posted paid caretaker vacancy requires it, and try one paid caretaker morning if offered. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept that role only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and utilities; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about learning another job at 58, but five years gives me a chance to watch a real caretaker. I want an older worker beside me when I learn a door lock, not a certificate in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the safety course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to fix a loose hinge under supervision and learn when to call a qualified repairer. A safety lesson should teach me when not to touch a wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Salma check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Salma (my wife) the full caretaker rota and the paid course hours before enrolling. We need the training week to pay like a working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us years to keep ordinary jobs paid while people learn the next one. I would ask the centre each year for a written junior rota and a real trainer on shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may be closer to ending full-time work by 2036, but I do not know what would pay the rent then. A little under three weeks saved makes today’s electricity bill more urgent than a distant plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking replacement-part calls and ask the supervisor each year for written paid junior hours and a real trainer on shift. In the first year after 2036, if my call hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid repair-counter job; I’d accept it only after a signed offer shows written weekly wage and hours covering rent and utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about 2036 and anxious about the next bill. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls does not pay the electricity due this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which yearly number matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the number of paid junior hours, not only how many replacement parts the centre processes. A busy screen can hide a thin wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family help with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children can visit for supper without becoming our income plan. Salma (my wife) and I will make decisions from the pay we actually have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a cheap system could answer the ordinary calls I have only just learned. A little under three weeks saved will not carry our rent while I learn a new trade. I would need early written notice, a posted paid opening with weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities, a paid trial, and employer-funded training on paid time if that opening requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether an older trainee gets to learn beside someone who has done the work. My brother taught me to sort a box of parts by touching the labels, not by guessing from a list.

headlineQuote: My brother taught me to sort a box of parts by touching the labels, not by guessing from a list.
portrait: At **58**, Ivan is a junior customer-service agent after secondary school and parts-counter work.
He and Salma rent with **under three weeks saved**, low pay and few nearby call jobs.
His **grown children** live separately, and he has no settled income plan for leaving full-time work.
He uses **AI occasionally** after a colleague shows him its limits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove ordinary calls before he learns another trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, rent-covering posted work, paid trial and funded required paid-time training would help.
